description:
In your kitchen, a German female and her offspring can make over 30,000 cockroaches in a year. This is a born-as guide to the German cockroach (Blattella germanica) in a house: the egg case, the crack, the night kitchen, how fast a kitchen gets crowded, what actually works against them, the force in a crack, the air in your house, and what people are told to do. Meatball lives all eight from the couch, with his dog, Noodle, as the stand-in and his cat, Sauce, as everybody else.

Checked facts in this video:
- Lead species is the German cockroach. German numbers stay on German. American cockroach (Periplaneta americana) numbers stay on American, and are tagged American in speech, on a card, or both. A line that says 'roaches' uses a species-general source and keeps that hedge.
- The German cockroach is the most common indoor species in California (and perhaps worldwide), especially in multi-unit housing (UC IPM). Keep 'perhaps.' It prefers kitchens and bathrooms, favoring warm (70° to 75°F), humid areas close to food, water, and dark areas for harborage. Severe infestations may spread to other parts of buildings. Of the cockroach species in California, it is the most persistent and troublesome, and may pose health concerns from food contamination and indoor allergens (UC IPM). They are commonly found in homes, apartments, condominiums, and commercial food establishments (Texas A&M).
- German and brownbanded cockroaches live and breed entirely indoors. American, Oriental, and Turkestan cockroaches live outdoors and can temporarily invade indoor spaces (UC IPM). This pest thrives in the presence of humans but does not occur outdoors (University of Kentucky). Adults are fully winged but rarely fly (Texas A&M). This video does not say they cannot fly.
- The female carries a light beige egg case, about 1/4 inch long, until 1 to 2 days before it hatches, when she drops it. Sometimes the egg case hatches while it is still being carried by the female. Each egg case contains about 30 young, and a female may produce a new egg case every few weeks (UC IPM). This is the spoken egg-case count. A different official page (UF/IFAS) describes the case as a tiny, brown, purse-shaped capsule, and gives a typical count of 30 to 40 eggs and a length of about 8 mm (~1/3 in). Those figures are not blended with UC IPM's 'about 30' and 'about 1/4 inch' in speech. University of Kentucky's 'up to 40' is also kept here, not spoken as one official number.
- Adults are light brown and about 1/2 inch long, with two dark stripes on the shield behind the head (University of Kentucky). A different official page puts adult bodies at 1/2 to 5/8 inches (Texas A&M). The two sizes are not averaged.
- Adult German cockroaches can hide in a crack 1/16 inch wide. Immature cockroaches tend to stay in even smaller cracks (UC IPM). That is a hide, not a body squeeze, and it is German-only.
- American cockroaches can squish their bodies to one-tenth of an inch, the height of two stacked pennies, and could slip through slits of one-tenth of an inch if highly motivated. They are about half an inch tall when they run freely. Not only can they squish themselves into one-tenth-of-an-inch crevices, but once inside they can run at high speed even when flattened in half. They can penetrate the tightest joints and seams in less than a second. In the study, American cockroaches withstood forces nearly 900 times their body weight without injury (Jayaram and Full, PNAS 2016, Periplaneta americana; also UC Berkeley News, 8 February 2016). Nearly 900 times is a maximum from compression tests, not the force of squeezing through a crevice. 'Without injury' is the study's wording, not a stunt. No dime comparison. The 1/16-inch German hide and the American squeeze, flattened run, and 900-times figure are not mixed.
- Even clean homes can become infested. The German cockroach is often introduced in infested grocery bags, beverage cartons, or furniture (University of Kentucky). They can gain entry by concealing themselves in groceries or luggage. Prevention is possible by inspecting boxes and bags as they are brought into a structure (Texas A&M). That is not a guarantee.
- During the day, roaches hide in warm, dark, moist areas. They come out at night to feed (UC IPM, species-general). Almost all cockroaches are nocturnal and tend to scatter when disturbed (UC IPM). Keep 'almost all.' At night they leave hiding places and search for food (University of Kentucky). Cockroaches will eat all human foods, plus many other items such as soap, toothpaste, glue, hair, excrement, and decaying organic matter (University of Kentucky). The German cockroach is omnivorous, eating table scraps, pet food, and even book bindings (UF/IFAS).
- The German cockroach has the fastest reproductive cycle of the common pest cockroaches: a single female and her offspring can produce over 30,000 individuals in a year (UC IPM). Keep German; female and her offspring; over 30,000; in a year. A different official page says a single mated female can produce thousands of new cockroaches in less than a year, and that German cockroaches are capable of producing several thousand offspring in less than a year (University of Kentucky). That is not the same claim, and it is not upgraded to 30,000.
- American cockroaches prefer warm and humid environments, usually with temperatures above 82°F. Each egg case contains about 12 young; a female and her offspring can produce over 800 cockroaches in one year (UC IPM). Those figures stay on American.
- The entire German life cycle is completed in about 100 days, but temperature, nutrition, and strain can change that. They breed continuously with overlapping generations. Under ideal conditions, population growth has been shown to be exponential. Actively growing field populations are about 80% nymphs and 20% adults (UF/IFAS).
- Good sanitation and exclusion are important; pesticides alone will not solve cockroach problems. When using insecticides, baits provide better control than sprays (UC IPM). Avoid foggers, bombs, or aerosol sprays: they can be hazardous and may repel and disperse cockroaches without actually killing them. Insecticide sprays do not provide long-term control (UC IPM). CDC also says to avoid sprays and foggers, as these can cause asthma attacks.
- Insecticide gels and bait stations placed near hiding areas can be effective if sources of food and water are removed. It may take 7 days or longer before you see fewer cockroaches. Female cockroaches with egg cases do very little feeding, so they are less likely to be immediately affected by a bait (UC IPM). Although good housekeeping is helpful, insecticides are usually necessary to eliminate infestations, especially of German cockroaches (University of Kentucky). Always read and follow label directions.
- Traps, bait stations, and other pesticide products can be used with low risk of exposure as long as they are kept out of reach of children and pets and used according to label directions (EPA). This video does not call baits safe. Controlling German cockroaches begins with sanitation. Exterior application of pesticides is unneeded for this indoor species. Bait stations should be used when tamper-resistant stations are needed (Texas A&M).
- EPA, on roaches, not as a German-only figure: although roaches can live up to one month without food, without water roaches can die in a week's time. That is a reason to drain dish water, wipe spills, and fix leaks. It is not a way to wipe out an infestation by itself. Seal up boxes and bags of food; roaches love cardboard boxes and can climb into them with ease (EPA).

- Indoor infestations of cockroaches are important sources of allergens and have been identified as risk factors for development of asthma in children, especially in multi-unit housing. Allergen levels have been correlated with cockroach density and with conditions that contribute to heavy infestations (UC IPM). Droppings or body parts of cockroaches and other pests can trigger asthma. Proteins in cockroach feces and saliva can cause allergic reactions or trigger asthma symptoms in some individuals (EPA). Keep 'can,' 'other pests,' and 'in some individuals.' Insecticides and pesticides can harm people too; try methods that pose less of a risk (EPA).
- Cockroaches and other pests are often found where food is eaten and crumbs are left behind. To control pests in your home, start with removing water and food, cleaning, and sealing cracks. Avoid using sprays and foggers, as these can cause asthma attacks (CDC).
- Not spoken in this video, kept here with their hedges: in extremely heavy infestations, German cockroaches have been reported to bite humans and feed on food residues on the faces of sleeping humans (UF/IFAS; not a casual hook). German cockroaches are believed to be capable of transmitting numerous disease-causing organisms such as Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, hepatitis virus, and coliform bacteria, and have been implicated in the spread of typhoid and dysentery (UC IPM). Keep 'believed to be capable' and 'implicated.'

General information, not a treatment plan for a specific house or a medical diagnosis. Follow the label. Keep products out of reach of children and pets. If asthma or an allergic reaction is a concern, follow official public-health guidance and your clinician.

Sources:
- UC IPM Pest Notes: Cockroaches, UC ANR Publication 7467: https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/cockroaches/
- University of Kentucky ENTFACT-614, Cockroach Elimination in Homes & Apartments, revised 3/26: https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef614
- Texas A&M Urban Entomology, German Cockroach: https://urbanentomology.tamu.edu/cockroaches/german-cockroach/
- UF/IFAS EENY-002 / IN128, German Cockroach, revised December 2024: https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN128/pdf
- UC Berkeley News, Robert Sanders, 8 February 2016, "Cockroach inspires robot that squeezes through cracks": https://news.berkeley.edu/2016/02/08/cockroach-inspires-robot-that-squeezes-through-cracks/
- EPA, Asthma Triggers: Gain Control: https://www.epa.gov/asthma/asthma-triggers-gain-control ; Do you really need to use a pesticide?: https://www.epa.gov/safepestcontrol/do-you-really-need-use-pesticide ; Smart Pest Control to Protect Your Health: https://www.epa.gov/pesticides/smart-pest-control-protect-your-health
- CDC, Help Your Patients Gain Control Over Asthma: https://www.cdc.gov/asthma/control/index.html
